text: The actors on screen stop performing and begin talking among themselves, then to the people watching them from the stalls. Word travels; a crowd forms on the pavement outside the Liberty; offices telephone one another to establish whose jurisdiction this is. The man finally sent to settle it is a censor in his fifties who spent an earlier life as a literary critic and a journalist, and who therefore knows exactly what he is being paid to stop. Wojciech Marczewski keeps the crisis administrative rather than cosmic, and keeps the film to eighty-seven minutes: the trouble is less that fiction has walked off the screen than that somebody must now write a report accounting for it. Poland, 1990. The fantasy has consequences for one man in the building, and he is the one who understands them.

The captain wants to know who is to blame for the collapse of an empire, and he has been given a great deal of unstructured time in which to work it out. He is held in a filtration camp in Crimea, the White Army having been evacuated, and the film never troubles to name him. What he returns to instead of politics is a brief affair from before all of this, as though the answer might be found in a few remembered days rather than in any argument about the state. Nikita Mikhalkov takes 175 minutes over that proposition, letting the affair keep its own tempo and the camp keep its own, so that the distance between the two becomes the point. A man with nothing to do but assign responsibility will assign it somewhere.

A woman flies in from Japan to Moscow because she has decided that the man she is looking for will be Russian. She is one thread among several: a couple who conduct their courtship dressed as anime characters, a secretary handed an indecent proposition by her employer, a graffiti artist chasing something he would call beauty, an ex-wife hired by her husband for an errand out of the ordinary. Anna Melikyan runs the stories alongside one another for 115 minutes without insisting that they add up, and the comedy comes from how differently each set of people would define the word all of them keep using. The arrangements get made in offices, on staircases, over the phone, practical settings for the least practical subject there is, and nobody is asked to agree with anybody else about terms.

Spring of 1794, and the plan requires two kinds of Pole who have never stood in the same line - the gentry and the peasantry - to take up arms for one cause. Tadeusz Kościuszko has come back to the country to arrange it. Beside him rides Domingo, a friend who was once a slave; behind him rides Dunin, a Russian cavalry captain intent on taking the general before the first shot of a national revolt is fired. Paweł Maślona builds this as a pursuit picture, 119 minutes of riding and recruiting, which puts the arguments about who owes what to whom into the mouths of men who are also being hunted, and who answer while moving. The uprising is a proposal, not yet a fact. Everything in the film turns on which Poles agree to it, and on what terms.

Music is the pretext, and in a town where Polish and Soviet uniforms pass one another daily, pretexts are in short supply. She is young, married to a Soviet officer, and living wherever his posting puts her; he is a Polish officer on his own ground, which turns out to be less of an advantage than it sounds. Waldemar Krzystek sets the affair inside Cold War machinery so ordinary that it barely registers as menace - permissions, transfers, the working assumption that someone nearby is in a position to report what he has seen. The period is carried by rooms and clothes rather than by announcements. What the film measures, over 114 minutes, is how much privacy two adults can manufacture when both of their lives are administered by other people.

Two men trained by the same country sit down at a chessboard, and only one of them still lives in it. Anatoly Karpov holds the world title; Viktor Korchnoi has recently emigrated from the USSR, which turns a sporting fixture into a matter on which the state has opinions. Alexey Sidorov gives this 145 minutes, an unusual allowance for an activity in which almost nothing visible occurs - a hand moves, a clock is pressed, two seated men think. The pressure has to be found in faces, in the seconds before a piece is committed, in the intervals when the board is left alone. That is the whole wager of the film: whether a camera can make a decision look like an event, and whether two men refusing to speak can hold the frame for as long as a match requires.

A journalist answers questions well on television, and while he is away the privileges that made his working life possible are quietly withdrawn. Nobody explains. His seminar is cancelled without a reason he can argue with; his wife of fifteen years, the mother of his two daughters, asks for a divorce and offers no account of why; and the two demolitions proceed by the same method, which is the coldest thing the film notices. Andrzej Wajda spends 131 minutes on a man who is very good with words as words stop working for him - every move he makes to repair the situation turns out to be the wrong one, and he cannot know which until it is made. Poland, 1978. He is being dismantled by people who never have to say so.

A young doctor has taken a posting at the far edge of central Asia on the understanding that the woman he intends to marry will follow him there. That is nearly the whole of the situation, and Mikheil Kalatozishvili holds it for 108 minutes without hurrying to complicate it. The work arrives on its own terms: whoever is injured, whoever is carried across open ground to the one person within reach who knows what to do about it. He improvises, because improvisation is what the distance leaves him. Waiting is the other occupation, and the film treats it as an occupation rather than an interval - a man keeping his competence and his expectations in good order in a place that has no particular use for either, and no intention of hurrying on his account.

An inn in the countryside, a night to be got through, and a door that anyone outside is free to knock on. The people gathered inside have run from a pogrom on the eve of the First World War, and with Cossacks nearby the fear in the room is less of an assault than of a neighbour's word - a name said aloud, a decision taken by somebody who is not in the building. Jerzy Kawalerowicz holds his 102 minutes close to that one house, which is a formal decision with a moral consequence: nobody can step outside the frame, so nobody is spared the argument going on inside it. What such a night does to prayer, to authority among the sheltering, to the ordinary business of eating while listening for hooves - that is where the film spends itself.

Two students take a summer internship on a trawler, which the dozen men already aboard understand to mean two more bodies in the way. What follows is largely work: hauling, gutting, cold water, a smell that gets into cloth and stays there. Boris Khlebnikov is interested in the distance between a young man's idea of going to sea and an older man's understanding of a wage, a season's pay, and a margin for error that the newcomers cannot yet read. The seascapes are severe, and the camera keeps returning from them to the deck, where rank is settled by competence and nobody has patience to explain a thing twice. 116 minutes on a rusty boat with a crew who like each other less than the job requires, and who are stuck with one another until the hold is full.

Two hundred and forty-five minutes, one marriage, and a country's fortunes running from the uprising of 1863 to the First World War. Barbara Ostrzeńska-Niechcic and Bogumił Niechcic belong to a noble family whose position is being worn away by a century that has stopped underwriting the arrangements they were raised inside. Jerzy Antczak adapts Maria Dabrowska closely and uses the running time for what running time is good at: letting a decision taken in one decade come due in the next, so that character registers as accumulation rather than as incident. A social thread and a private one run through the film and keep crossing. Nothing in it looks like a turning point while it is happening, which is the argument for its length.

One face carries all four men - an army officer, a college instructor, a priest, a drug dealer - and the actor wearing it also wrote the script and directed the film. Jerzy Stuhr sets each of them a version of the same test in a different key: a student announces her love to her teacher, an eleven-year-old announces her parentage to a priest, an old lover reappears to an officer, a dealer taken prisoner has to decide how far his wife can be trusted with what he has hidden. Eighty-seven minutes, four compartments, one performer moving between them, which makes the casting the argument: these are not four types but one man under four sets of rules. Krzysztof Kieslowski, in whose films Stuhr had acted, advised on the screenplay. The comedy sits in the timing of each disclosure.

Daniel is valued in his village for exactly as long as the causes he takes up are the ones the village already holds. He is also in love with Olek from next door, who is not prepared to be known that way, so the two of them meet where nobody is looking. When a teenager in the same community dies after being hounded for the same reason, Daniel proposes that everyone walk the Stations of the Cross together in the dead friend's name - a request framed in the parish's own language, which makes it difficult to refuse as something foreign. Łukasz Gutt keeps this to ninety minutes and keeps it local: one parish, a set of neighbours, a form of prayer they all claim. Whether the village walks with him is a question about the village.

A rented bed in an old woman's house and a job felling trees: this is what a young poet takes in place of the city he has decided against. He is after a plainer order of things, and the village supplies an order, though not the one he had in mind and not one arranged for his convenience. Witold Leszczyński gives it 82 minutes, brisk for a story whose real subject is a man learning by degrees that plain living has politics of its own - who is owed labour, who gets which bed, who decides what a stranger is for. The ache comes from the symmetry: he has renounced a world that was never much interested in him, in favour of one that is interested only in whether he can work. What his poems are worth in that arrangement stays unsettled.
